passage:
The metro carriage swayed, and every seat was full. Ritu, twenty-four, noticed Yogesh Uncle at the door, one hand on the pole and the other on a cane. His knuckles were pale. Before he could ask, she stood and said, "Uncle, please sit here."
"You keep it, beta," he said.
"I get off in two stops, please."
He sat with a small sigh. A teenager across the aisle looked up, then stood for a woman carrying a toddler. A man moved his bag from the seat next to her. The whole coach seemed to loosen. Ritu held the rail and felt warm, though her legs were tired.

qa.q: What was Yogesh Uncle holding in his hands?
qa.a: He held the pole with one hand and a cane in the other.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling as she held the rail after giving up her seat?
qa.a: Ritu felt warm and content, even though her legs were tired.

qa.q: What did Ritu do that made a difference for others in the coach?
qa.a: She offered the seat before being asked, and the teenager and another man soon copied by giving up a seat and moving a bag.

qa.q: How might Yogesh Uncle have felt standing at the door with a cane?
qa.a: He was probably tired and unsteady, shown by his pale knuckles, and he may have been reluctant to accept help at first, saying 'You keep it, beta'.

grounding: A young commuter offers a seat to an elder before being asked, and others copy the kindness.

"Rukmini, take my seat," said Hafsa, already standing.
"I'm fine, really."
"You've been holding that bag and the baby since Sector 9. Please."
"Are you sure?"
"I get off at the next stop anyway."
Rukmini lowered herself onto the seat with a grateful sigh. "Thank you, Hafsa."
Across the aisle, a man in a grey shirt had seen it. He stood and gestured to a woman with a walking stick. "Please, ma'am."
Hafsa smiled. "Catching, isn't it?"
"I'll do the same next time," said Rukmini, with her hand on her belly.
The conductor called out the next stop, and Hafsa held the pole.

qa.q: Since which sector had Rukmini been holding the bag?
qa.a: Rukmini had been holding the bag since Sector 9.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she sat down?
qa.a: Rukmini felt grateful and relieved, since she sighed with thanks.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that led to others copying?
qa.a: Hafsa stood and offered a seat before Rukmini asked, and a man in a grey shirt then gave his seat to a woman with a walking stick.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have felt when the man in the grey shirt gave up his seat too?
qa.a: Hafsa probably felt pleased and a little amused, smiling and saying, "Catching, isn't it?"

grounding: A young commuter offers a seat to a pregnant woman without waiting to be asked, and others soon copy.

passage:
On the Delhi metro last month, I got a seat at Rajiv Chowk after a long day. I'm Rehana, and my feet ached. At the next station, an elderly man got on with a walking stick. Lalit Uncle, I found out later.
Nobody moved. People looked at their phones. He held the pole with both hands, swaying.
I stood up and said, "Uncle, please sit." He smiled and sat. That was it.
But then something happened. At the next station, a young man got up for a pregnant woman. Two stops later, a college girl gave her seat to a man with a crutch. It spread down the coach like a wave.
Lalit Uncle said, "In my day we did this without thinking. Nice to see it."
I stood the rest of the way. My feet still ached. But I felt lighter.

qa.q: Where did Rehana get a seat?
qa.a: She got a seat at Rajiv Chowk.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel standing the rest of the way?
qa.a: Rehana's feet still ached, but Rehana felt lighter and happy after offering the seat.

qa.q: What happened after Rehana gave up the seat?
qa.a: Others copied her: a young man got up for a pregnant woman and a college girl gave her seat to a man with a crutch, showing kindness spreads.

qa.q: How might Lalit Uncle have felt when he sat down?
qa.a: Lalit Uncle probably felt relieved and pleased, glad to see young people offer seats.

grounding: A young commuter offers a seat to an elder without being asked, and the kindness spreads as others copy it.

passage:
Commuter-awareness volunteer's note, Bus 522, Monday morning.
The bus was packed. At the hospital stop, Jyoti, a young woman who was visibly pregnant, got on and stood near the door, holding her bag against her.
Dhruv, 24, sitting near the front with a laptop bag, noticed her at once. He stood up without waiting and said, "Please, take this seat." She thanked him and sat.
What I noted next: a man across the aisle, who had been looking at his phone, stood up for an elderly woman a stop later. A schoolboy made space for a man with a cane.
When I spoke to Dhruv as he got off, he said, "My mother had a hard time on buses when she was pregnant with my sister. I always remember that."
Next step: I will share this example in our campaign posters.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti get on?
qa.a: Jyoti got on at the hospital stop.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv give up his seat so quickly?
qa.a: Dhruv felt caring and understanding, remembering how hard buses were for his mother when she was pregnant.

qa.q: What did Dhruv's kindness lead to?
qa.a: Others copied it: a man stood for an elderly woman and a schoolboy made space for a man with a cane, showing kindness is contagious.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel when Dhruv offers the seat?
qa.a: Jyoti would probably feel relieved and grateful, no longer standing on a packed bus.

grounding: A volunteer's note shows a young commuter giving a seat to a pregnant woman without being asked, and others quickly copying the kindness.

passage:
Wednesday
Local train home, 6 p.m. rush. I had a window seat. At Dadar, a blind man got on with a white cane, and the crowd pushed him around.
I remembered my Nani saying, "Don't wait for someone to ask. By then it's too late." So I stood and said, "Sir, there's a seat here, one step to your left." I guided his hand to the seat. He said, "Thank you, beta."
My friend Jatin, standing next to me, was quiet. Then, at the next stop, he gave his seat to a lady with a baby. After that, a woman gave hers to an old man.
Jatin said, "I never thought of doing that till I saw you."
I stood all the way to Thane with my bag digging into my shoulder. Honestly, it didn't matter.
Ishita

qa.q: What did the blind man carry?
qa.a: He carried a white cane.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel standing all the way to Thane?
qa.a: Ishita felt content and warm, not minding the bag digging in, after helping the man.

qa.q: What did Ishita's action lead to?
qa.a: Jatin gave his seat to a lady with a baby, and another woman gave hers to an old man, showing that kindness spreads.

qa.q: How might Jatin see his own habits after that day?
qa.a: Jatin seems to realise he had never thought of giving his seat, and may now do it without waiting.

grounding: A young commuter offers a seat to a blind man without being asked, and her friend and others soon copy the kindness.
